body.text: Earlier this week, the Trump administration announced new restrictions on access to the most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, targeting Southeast Asia’s role in providing computing power to Chinese companies.

According to an interim final rule (IFR) released on Monday by the U.S. Department of Commerce, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil will need a U.S. government license to export, re-export, or transfer advanced AI chips.

In a statement, the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said that the rule was “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.”

The IFR (full text available here) is intended “to prevent foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.” It stated that the five countries of concern “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of computing capacity to China.

The rule requires overseas data centers that provide a significant volume of computing power to companies headquartered in China to obtain U.S. export licenses for semiconductor chips by mid-February or face future export restrictions. U.S.-headquartered companies will be exempt from the restrictions as long as they report their shipments of chips.

Commerce said that it will also “be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries.” These include import restrictions, new license requirements, a potential downgrade of the country’s status in the U.S. export control regime, and potential sanctions.

The rule is set to have a significant impact on Southeast Asia’s booming data center industry. The past few years have seen a surge in construction in data centers, including those that house the semiconductors needed to train and develop AI models. This has been driven in large part by surging demand from Chinese customers, including tech giants like Alibaba and ByteDance, whose access to cutting-edge Nvidia chips has been obstructed by existing U.S. export controls.

CNBC cited estimates from the Washington-based Institute for Progress that showed around three-quarters of China’s overseas AI capacity – 505.8 megawatts of AI capacity out of a total of 794.2 megawatts – was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026.

The region’s position in the global chip trade has drawn the scrutiny of U.S. lawmakers for some time. Initially, concerns centered on the allegation that firms based in Southeast Asia were purchasing U.S.-manufactured frontier chips, such as Nvidia’s Nvidia’s Blackwell or H200 chips, and smuggling them to Chinese end-users.

Attention has recently shifted to the renting by Chinese firms of computing capacity in Southeast Asian data centers. One of those is the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang has been accused of being a Chinese spy. Pressure for tighter controls on these sorts of firms has grown since Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang and resigned on November 12,

What impact are the new restrictions likely to have in Southeast Asia? Analysts say that the they could stall ongoing projects and potentially impact the region’s desire to become a trusted AI hub. The new restrictions will likely make building and operating new data centers “slower and costlier,” Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.

Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions. The country has attracted nearly $100 billion in data center investments since 2021, and according to one recent analysis, has become “the primary scale-out location for data center expansion in the region,” due to its abundant land, low power costs, and proximity to Singapore. The country’s data centers, most of which are centered in Johor, also rely particularly heavily on Chinese customers, meaning that new data centers may be left with unleased capacity. Singapore, meanwhile, remains the region’s “command node – the place where latency-sensitive financial and enterprise workloads run, where hyperscaler regional headquarters sit, and where regulatory frameworks are most mature.”

Matthias Hendrichs, a Singapore-based advisor to AI companies, told Channel News Asia (CNA) that companies with Chinese links could face “delays of months” for new projects. “Nobody wants to commit hundreds of millions to a data center without knowing whether they can get the chips to fill it,” he said.

At the same time, the effects in Malaysia are unlikely to be uniform, Ming San Soong, an analyst at MBSB Research in Malaysia, told Reuters, suggesting that the rules could end up creating a two-tier industry.

“Owner-operated campuses serving established U.S. hyperscalers should be better placed, while facilities reliant on Chinese AI customers or opaque GPU-as-a-Service arrangements may face longer licensing and customer-verification processes,” he said.

The new policy is likely to test the regulatory regimes in each of the four nations, which differ considerably. Maria Monica Wihardja, a fellow at ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told CNA that Singapore and Malaysia “have export control laws or strategic trade management frameworks,” while Thailand has set up a framework but had not yet fully implemented it. Indonesia, meanwhile, has no dedicated framework and relies on “scattered customs, import-export and sector-specific laws.”

Singapore has been proactive in responding to the new U.S. rules. In a joint statement on Tuesday, the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and Ministry of Digital Development and Information said that they were “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.

“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” they said. “We have also been engaging the relevant U.S. authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”

Meanwhile, Malaysia’s Trade Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said yesterday that Malaysia’s data center operators should comply with the new U.S. restrictions. “If you want that GPU chip for your data center that comes from the U.S., you have to comply with the U.S. rules and regulations. Whoever is willing to comply, comply, then you can buy the chip,” he told reporters on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

He said that the government had yet to receive documentary evidence showing that data center tenants had traded or re-exported advanced chips to China. “If they re-export, we want to know who, and they have to come up with the manifests they submitted. Only then can we proceed. We cannot simply accuse,” he said.
Thailand’s Ministry of Commerce also says that it has ordered an assessment of the new U.S. restrictions.

It currently remains to be seen how thorough Washington’s policing of its new rules will be. That could end up being the difference between whether it creates a small obstruction on Southeast Asia’s road to AI centrality or the beginning of the end for the region’s data center boomtimes.
